column112: The interactions social_science × paper_inequality_mentions_3_years and social_science × news_inequality_mentions_3_years, both positive, form the temporal core of this theory and are general mechanisms that operate across inequality domains. I theorize these through the concept of discursive opportunity structure, which captures how the broader scholarly and societal attention environment alters the likelihood of engaging inequality, but only for papers in disciplines equipped to capitalize on that environment. When recent academic literature has paid heightened attention to inequality—whether racial, gender, or economic—a dense, citing, and intellectually vital conversation is underway. This creates receptive conditions: reviewers are familiar with and favorably disposed toward inequality frameworks, special issues and edited volumes provide concrete publication venues, and the perceived importance of inequality scholarship is elevated. Social science papers are uniquely positioned to join and extend this conversation because they possess the theoretical vocabularies, methodological toolkits, and professional incentive structures that make inequality a legitimate object of inquiry. A paper in natural science or engineering, regardless of its authors' personal interests, lacks the disciplinary infrastructure to enter this conversation; the discursive opportunity structure does not extend across the epistemological boundary. The parallel mechanism for news attention operates through societal relevance amplification. When inequality surges in public discourse—whether through social movements like #MeToo, political controversies over equal pay, or catalyzing events that draw attention to gender-based violence—a generalized societal concern with gender hierarchy emerges. This societal energy does not affect all academic fields uniformly; it is filtered through disciplinary apparatus. Social scientists are professionally socialized to respond to problems of public concern, and the perceived relevance and fundability of gender inequality research increases precisely when the public cares most. Social science thus serves as the institutional translator that converts societal attention into formal scholarly knowledge. The positive interaction for academic attention and the positive interaction for news attention represent, respectively, the internal and external faces of this translational function: social science amplifies the effects of both scholarly momentum and public concern. The female × social_science interaction, with a negative sign, is best understood through three complementary mechanisms, which together form a differential diagnosticity framework. The first and most important mechanism is a ceiling effect. Social science is such a powerful positive predictor of gender inequality discourse that the baseline probability within this disciplinary context is already very high. When a social science paper is already highly likely to discuss gender inequality regardless of author demographics, the marginal predictive contribution of any additional feature—including female authorship—is necessarily compressed. The female effect can only operate where there is variance to explain, and social science leaves little room for it. The second mechanism concerns baseline diagnosticity outside social science. In natural science, engineering, and other non-social-science fields, studying gender inequality is a rare, counter-normative act that deviates from the dominant intellectual agenda of the discipline. When a paper in these fields does engage gender inequality, author gender becomes a highly informative signal because it helps explain the deviation. A woman in a male-dominated engineering department writing about sexism in STEM is likely doing so precisely because her personal experience in that context makes the topic urgent and unavoidable; her authorship is deeply diagnostic of the paper's content in a way that a female sociologist's authorship is not, because the latter is simply doing what many scholars—men and women alike—do in her field. The third mechanism introduces a dynamic of within-discipline heterogeneity and strategic self-presentation outside social science. In non-social-science fields, where studying gender is unusual and may carry professional risk, the women who do so are a self-selected group with particularly strong motivation. This selection effect tightens the female-gender inequality link precisely where the baseline is lowest. Meanwhile, within social science, many male scholars study gender inequality as a legitimate and even prestigious specialization, further eroding the gender diagnosticity of the topic within that disciplinary context. The negative interaction thus does not imply that social science suppresses female engagement with gender inequality—the main effect of female remains positive overall—but rather that the predictive value of knowing an author's gender is greatest in the disciplinary contexts where gender inequality scholarship is scarcest and therefore most informative as a signal of authorial motivation. The likelihood that a paper discusses gender inequality depends not only on stable features of discipline and authorship but on when the paper enters the scholarly conversation relative to shifting currents of academic and public attention, and on how the diagnosticity of author identity varies inversely with the disciplinary baseline. This framework preserves the core insight that female authorship is a robust positive predictor of gender inequality discourse, while explaining why its marginal predictive power is greatest not where such discourse is most common, but where it is most unexpected.

My revised theory for gender inequality generates several testable claims using the available features. I propose three empirical tests that target distinct mechanisms: the differential diagnosticity of female authorship across disciplinary contexts, the asymmetric channeling of inequality concern, and the temporal responsiveness of gender inequality discourse to societal events.

---

**Test 1: Differential Diagnosticity of Female Authorship Across Disciplinary Baselines**

My revised theory claims that the female effect on studying gender inequality is strongest where the disciplinary baseline is lowest—that is, female authorship is most diagnostic in fields where gender inequality discourse is rare. This implies a negative relationship between a discipline's baseline probability of discussing gender inequality and the size of the female coefficient within that discipline.

*Operationalization:* I would divide the dataset into fine-grained disciplinary categories using the three binary discipline indicators. The key contrast is between **social_science** and **non-social_science** (natural_science + engineering_and_technology). I would estimate separate logistic regression models for each broad domain:

> Gender_Inequality ~ female + black + asian + hispanic_and_other + white + authors_race_diversity_score + country_race_diversity_score + num_authors + paper_inequality_mentions_3_years + year_of_publication

estimated separately for social_science = 1 and social_science = 0.

*Supporting results:* My theory predicts that the coefficient on `female` will be **substantially larger** in the non-social-science subsample than in the social science subsample. I would also plot the predicted probability of discussing gender inequality across the range of female share for both disciplinary domains. The slope of this curve should be visibly steeper for non-social-science papers, illustrating the greater diagnosticity of author gender where the topic is rare. If the coefficients were equal or the social science coefficient were larger, this would falsify the differential diagnosticity mechanism and support my original amplification model.

---

**Test 2: Asymmetric Channeling Across Inequality Axes**

My revised theory, incorporating the negative female × social_science interaction for gender inequality, implies a specific form of cross-axis channeling that differs from the racial inequality case. For gender, the negative interaction arises from a ceiling effect and differential diagnosticity, not from a redirection of concern toward another axis. This yields a clear empirical prediction: unlike the racial inequality case, where I theorized that female concern is channeled *toward* gender within social science, here the female effect on gender inequality is simply less informative in social science but not replaced by a stronger effect on another axis. This can be tested by directly comparing interaction patterns across the two outcomes.

*Operationalization:* Using the same dataset, I would construct both outcome variables—racial inequality mention and gender inequality mention—and estimate parallel models:

> Racial_Inequality ~ female × social_science + [controls]

> Gender_Inequality ~ female × social_science + [controls]

*Supporting results:* My theory predicts that the **female × social_science** interaction will be **negative for both outcomes**, but for subtly different reasons. For racial inequality, the mechanism is cross-axis channeling (female concern directed toward gender within social science) combined with a ceiling effect. For gender inequality, the mechanism is primarily a ceiling effect and differential diagnosticity. The critical test is whether the *magnitude* of the negative interaction differs across outcomes. If the interaction is more strongly negative for racial inequality than for gender inequality, this supports the channeling interpretation: women in social science redirect their inequality concern toward their most directly experienced axis (gender), suppressing the race effect beyond what the ceiling effect alone would predict. If the interactions are of similar magnitude, the pure ceiling effect interpretation is better supported. I would also test a three-way interaction—female × social_science × inequality_type—in a stacked dataset, predicting a significant three-way term indicating that the dampening effect of social science on the female coefficient is stronger for racial inequality than for gender inequality.

---

**Test 3: Temporal Responsiveness to Gender-Specific Societal Events**

My revised theory claims that social science uniquely translates societal attention into scholarly output on gender inequality through the societal relevance amplification mechanism. A natural experiment can test this by exploiting the temporal variation in public attention to gender issues.

*Operationalization:* The 2000–2020 window contains a major catalyzing event for gender inequality discourse: the emergence of the #MeToo movement in October 2017. I would construct a binary variable `post_metoo` equal to 1 for publication years 2018–2020, and 0 for a comparable pre-event window (2014–2016), omitting 2017 as a transitional year. I would estimate:

> Gender_Inequality ~ social_science + natural_science + engineering_and_technology + post_metoo + social_science × post_metoo + natural_science × post_metoo + [author demographic controls + paper_inequality_mentions_3_years]

*Supporting results:* My theory predicts a **positive and significant coefficient** on **social_science × post_metoo**, indicating that social science papers were substantially more likely to discuss gender inequality in the #MeToo era than before, relative to non-social-science papers. I would expect the natural_science × post_metoo and engineering_and_technology × post_metoo interactions to be near zero and non-significant, confirming that the translational function is discipline-specific. Additionally, to distinguish the societal relevance mechanism from the scholarly momentum mechanism, I would include `paper_inequality_mentions_3_years` as a control. If the social_science × post_metoo interaction remains significant after controlling for recent scholarly attention, this indicates a direct pathway from societal events to scholarly output that operates independently of the academic conversation's internal momentum—precisely the institutional translation function my theory posits.
column116:
My revised theory points to several additional variables that would enable more precise tests of its core mechanisms. I propose three categories of variables not currently available.

---

Category 1: Author Gender Salience and Self-Reported Identity

Variable: A measure of the proportion of female authors on the team based on self-reported gender rather than name-based imputation would strengthen measurement validity. More importantly, I would want a measure of gender identity salience for each author—perhaps proxied by whether they have served on gender equity committees, signed diversity statements, or affiliated with women-in-STEM organizations.

Empirical test: My differential diagnosticity theory implies that women who study gender inequality in male-dominated fields are a self-selected group with particularly strong motivation. I would test whether, among women in non-social-science fields, those who study gender inequality score higher on measures of gender identity salience than those who do not, and whether this selection effect is weaker or absent in social science. If women who study gender in engineering are systematically more engaged with gender advocacy than their peers who do not, this supports the selection-based diagnosticity mechanism. In social science, where studying gender is more common and less tied to personal identity salience, this correlation should be weaker.

---

Category 2: Institutional Gender Composition and Climate

Variable: Department-level or institution-level measures of gender composition among faculty and graduate students, and survey-based measures of departmental climate regarding gender diversity (e.g., perceived support for gender research, experiences of sexism).

Empirical test: My theory suggests that female authorship is most diagnostic of gender inequality research in fields where women are underrepresented and where the climate is less supportive. I would test a cross-level interaction: the female coefficient on studying gender inequality should be larger in departments with fewer women and in departments with poorer climate ratings. In highly gender-diverse, supportive departments, gender inequality may be studied by scholars of all genders, reducing the diagnosticity of any individual author's gender. In male-dominated, less supportive departments, the women who persist and study gender are a highly selected group for whom the topic is personally salient. I would also test whether the #MeToo movement differentially affected scholars in departments with different gender climates—the societal relevance amplification mechanism may be strongest where the local environment makes the societal conversation feel most personally relevant.

---

Category 3: Author Disciplinary Mobility and Interdisciplinarity

Variable: A measure of whether authors have moved between disciplines over their careers (e.g., a PhD in one field and a faculty appointment in another), and the interdisciplinarity of their publication record (e.g., the diversity of journals in which they publish).

Empirical test: My theory invokes comparative sensibility as a mechanism for Asian authorship—the idea that navigating multiple cultural frameworks makes gender visible as constructed. This mechanism has a disciplinary analogue: scholars who move between disciplines may similarly perceive taken-for-granted disciplinary assumptions about gender more acutely. I would test whether disciplinary mobility predicts engagement with gender inequality, and whether this effect is stronger for scholars whose mobility spans the social science/natural science boundary. A physicist who also publishes in science and technology studies, for example, may be uniquely positioned to see how gender operates in scientific institutions. If disciplinary boundary-crossers are more likely to study gender inequality, this would extend the comparative sensibility logic from the cultural to the disciplinary domain. I would also test whether the Asian authorship effect on gender inequality research is moderated by whether the scholar was trained in Asia versus the West, distinguishing the "embedded in Asian societies" pathway from the "diaspora comparative perspective" pathway.

Expected results supporting my theory: Across these tests, my revised theory would be supported by evidence that (a) women studying gender in male-dominated fields show stronger gender identity salience and select into the topic based on personal experience, (b) the diagnosticity of female authorship for gender research is strongest in departments with fewer women and poorer gender climate, and (c) disciplinary boundary-crossers, like cultural boundary-crossers, display heightened attunement to gender as a constructed and variable social arrangement. These patterns would collectively validate the differential diagnosticity framework and the broader theoretical architecture linking social location, institutional context, and temporal currents to the production of knowledge about gender inequality.

column30: My ranking rests on the premise that whether a paper discusses racial inequality is determined jointly by disciplinary opportunity, temporal salience, and author standpoint, in roughly that order of force. Disciplinary scope comes first because the inequality keywords are essentially the working vocabulary of the social sciences; a journal's scope sets the boundary conditions for whether such language can plausibly appear at all, which is why social_science carries the strongest positive sign and engineering_and_technology the clearest negative one (with only a modest weakening from the recent rise of algorithmic-fairness work that imports "racial bias" into computer science). I rank the two contextual trend variables highly because the production of academic knowledge is not insulated from its environment: paper_inequality_mentions_3_years captures intellectual momentum and agenda-setting within the field—rising attention makes the topic more citable, fundable, and legitimate—while news_inequality_mentions_3_years captures the broader public attention cycle that spills into scholarly agendas with a short lag (e.g., surges around high-profile racial-justice events). I place the within-academia signal above the news signal on the assumption that scholars respond more directly to their own field's conversation than to media coverage. The inclusion of black with a positive sign reflects a standpoint-and-homophily logic: scholars whose own group experiences racial marginalization are disproportionately motivated to study it, so author identity proxies for topical self-selection. The key assumptions underlying all of this are that journal scope reliably constrains topical content, that attention to inequality diffuses across the news–academy boundary, and that the name-and-country-based identity inferences—though noisy—are accurate enough in aggregate to preserve the true direction of the standpoint effect.

My reaction is one of partial validation alongside two genuine surprises. The model confirmed my top pick—social_science (+) ranked first exactly as I predicted—and validated black (+), which I had ranked third, though it landed fifth. The broad logic of disciplinary opportunity plus author standpoint survived contact with the data.

The divergences are instructive. First, the most striking surprise is female_score (+) at rank 2, a feature I did not place in my racial top five at all. I had reserved the standpoint-and-homophily logic for own-group identity (Black authors studying racial inequality) and treated gender as belonging to the gender task. The data suggest a "double standpoint" or general-marginalization effect: women, regardless of race, are disproportionately drawn to inequality scholarship of all kinds, so female authorship proxies for a broader disposition toward equity-oriented research rather than gender-specific topics. There may also be a compositional confound—gender studies, social work, and the equity-oriented subfields that house racial-inequality work are themselves female-dominated—so female_score partly captures disciplinary sub-location my coarse social_science binary missed.

Second, both country_race_diversity_score (+, rank 3) and asian (+, rank 4) outperformed my expectations—I had ranked the temporal trend variables and engineering above them. This points to a mechanism I under-weighted: the demographic-exposure channel. Authors from racially diverse countries, and Asian authors (often internationally mobile and experiencing racialization in their host academic systems), may have heightened salience of race through lived heterogeneity, not just own-group membership. I had framed standpoint narrowly as belonging-to-the-marginalized-group; the data favor a broader "exposure to racial difference" account.

Third, and most humbling, my two temporal/contextual variables (paper_ and news_inequality_mentions) did not appear in the top five despite my ranking them second and fifth. I likely overestimated cross-sectional importance: because these variables move slowly and are shared across all papers in a given window, they have low discriminating power between papers within the sample even if they matter in absolute terms. Gini-based importance rewards features that split individual papers apart, and author-composition variables vary far more across papers than a year-level trend does. This is a measurement-vs-mechanism distinction I should have anticipated—a variable can be causally real yet uninformative for within-sample classification.

Overall: my disciplinary intuition was sound, my narrow framing of standpoint was too restrictive (author composition broadly, especially female and diversity/exposure, matters more than I allowed), and I conflated absolute causal importance with cross-sectional predictive power for the temporal features.
column44: Whether a paper discusses racial inequality is governed by three forces—disciplinary opportunity, author standpoint broadly construed, and temporal salience—but the machine-learning evidence prompts me to substantially reweight the second and reconceive its mechanism. My reaction is a mix of strong vindication on the structure of the interactions and one genuinely counterintuitive sign that forces me to rethink a relationship I thought I understood.

First, the vindication: my second-ranked interaction, social_science × paper_inequality_mentions_3_years (+), came in first exactly as predicted and with the predicted positive sign. This confirms the core complementarity logic—temporal salience can only convert into actual racial-inequality papers within disciplines that possess the vocabulary and venues to absorb it. Even more encouraging, social_science × news_inequality_mentions_3_years (+) ranked second, validating the same conditioning mechanism for the public-attention channel, which I had specified in my causal diagram (news salience feeding intra-academic momentum, both amplified within social science). Notably, these two interaction terms surfaced as highly important even though the main effects of the temporal variables were weak—which is itself theoretically meaningful: the attention variables matter not on their own but interactively, by conditioning on disciplinary opportunity. That resolves part of my Race.11 puzzle. A slow-moving, low-variance trend has little standalone discriminating power, but its interaction with discipline splits papers effectively because it only "fires" in the right disciplinary context.

The real surprise is the third interaction, female × social_science (−). I had predicted social_science × black as my top interaction with a positive sign, expecting standpoint effects to be amplified within social science. The data reverse this intuition for gender: female authorship's effect on racial-inequality discussion is attenuated, not amplified, inside social science. On reflection, this makes sense as a redundancy/saturation effect rather than a contradiction. In my Race.12 revision I argued that female_score partly proxies for location in equity-oriented subfields. But once a paper is already known to be social science, that proxy becomes largely redundant—the disciplinary context has already "used up" much of the signal that female authorship was standing in for. The marginal informational contribution of female authorship is therefore largest outside social science, where a female-authored paper in, say, a technical or natural-science field is a strong and rare signal that the paper has deliberately turned toward inequality themes. In other words, the two variables are substitutes at the margin, not complements: each is most diagnostic when the other is absent. This is the same logic that explains negative interactions generally—ceiling effects and informational overlap—and it cautions me that my blanket assumption of multiplicative complementarity across all standpoint × discipline pairs was too strong. Complementarity holds for attention × discipline (both needed, neither sufficient) but substitution holds for female-as-subfield-proxy × discipline (overlapping signals).
column54: My updated theory of second-order interactions distinguishes between two structurally different ways features combine—complementarity and substitution—rather than assuming uniform multiplicative amplification as I did initially. The dominant pattern is complementarity between temporal attention and disciplinary opportunity: social_science × paper_inequality_mentions_3_years and social_science × news_inequality_mentions_3_years are both strongly positive because rising attention to inequality, whether originating inside academia or in the public sphere, can only convert into actual racial-inequality papers within disciplines that possess the vocabulary, venues, and legitimacy to absorb it. Neither input is sufficient alone—a salience surge is inert in technical fields, and disciplinary fit needs an activating climate—so they multiply. This interactive structure also resolves a puzzle from the main-effects stage: the temporal variables had weak standalone discriminating power precisely because their causal force is conditional, expressed only through interaction with discipline, so they surface as important interaction terms even while being weak main effects. The crucial revision concerns standpoint × discipline, where I now recognize a substitution rather than complementarity logic for variables that proxy disciplinary location. The female × social_science interaction is negative because female authorship partly stands in for being situated in equity-oriented, female-dominated subfields; once a paper is already identified as social science, that proxy becomes largely redundant, so female authorship's marginal informational contribution is largest outside social science, where a female-authored technical paper is a rare and strong signal of a deliberate turn toward inequality themes. The two variables are therefore substitutes at the margin—each most diagnostic when the other is absent—driven by informational overlap and ceiling effects. The unifying revised assumption is that whether an interaction is positive or negative depends on the informational relationship between the two features: when they capture distinct, jointly necessary inputs (attention and opportunity), they complement and the sign is positive; when one feature is partly a proxy for the other (female authorship for equity-subfield location, which discipline already encodes), they substitute and the sign is negative. My revised theory makes three testable main-effect claims: (1) disciplinary scope is the master driver; (2) author composition operates through a broadened standpoint logic with three distinct channels—general equity-disposition (female), exposure to racial difference (country diversity, Asian share), and own-group membership (Black share); and (3) the temporal-attention variables are causally real but low cross-sectional discriminators. Here are empirical tests for each.

Test 1 — Disciplinary master-effect (regression).
Estimate a logistic regression of discusses_racial_inequality on social_science, natural_science, and engineering_and_technology (one omitted as baseline), with all author-composition and temporal controls. Supporting result: social_science carries a large positive coefficient, engineering_and_technology a significant negative one, and the discipline dummies alone yield substantially higher pseudo-R² / classification gain than any other feature block. This confirms scope as the dominant constraint.

Test 2 — Disentangling the three standpoint channels (regression with simultaneous entry).
Regress the outcome on female, asian, black, hispanic_and_other, and country_race_diversity_score simultaneously, plus discipline controls. My theory predicts that female, asian, country_race_diversity_score, AND black each retain independent positive coefficients—because they tap distinct mechanisms rather than a single underlying signal. Supporting result: all four remain positive and significant when entered together (no single channel absorbs the others). A particularly strong test: country_race_diversity_score should stay positive even after controlling for the individual race shares, indicating that exposure to diversity matters beyond own-group composition.

Test 3 — Adjudicating "disposition" vs. "subfield-location" for female (mediation via discipline).
My revised theory says female_score partly proxies equity-oriented subfield location. Compare the female coefficient with vs. without discipline controls. Supporting result: the female coefficient shrinks noticeably once social_science is controlled (consistent with partial subfield-location proxying) but remains positive and significant (consistent with a residual genuine disposition effect). Full attenuation to zero would favor pure subfield-location; no attenuation would favor pure disposition; partial attenuation supports my dual-mechanism claim.

Test 4 — Exposure-channel placebo/specificity check.
Contrast country_race_diversity_score against authors_race_diversity_score. My exposure logic emphasizes lived heterogeneity in one's origin context. Supporting result: both diversity measures are positive, but their pattern is informative—if exposure-through-origin drives the effect, country_race_diversity_score should be robustly positive; if it were merely team composition, authors_race_diversity_score would dominate. Either way, a positive diversity effect net of individual race shares supports the exposure channel over pure own-group standpoint.

Test 5 — Temporal variables: causally real but low-variance (natural experiment using year_of_publication).
Code a post-2014 indicator (capturing the rise of large-scale racial-justice mobilization and the sharp increase in inequality attention in the mid-2010s) using year_of_publication. Two complementary analyses:
(a) Absolute-effect test: the share of papers discussing racial inequality should rise significantly post-2014, and news_/paper_inequality_mentions_3_years should be higher in the post period—confirming the variables are causally relevant in absolute terms.
(b) Low-discrimination test: despite (a), adding the two temporal mention variables to a within-period classifier should yield only a small improvement in cross-sectional fit (AUC/Gini) relative to author-composition features—confirming that slow-moving, near-constant-within-window trends carry little paper-level discriminating power. Re-estimate Test 2 separately within social_science papers and within non-social-science papers. Supporting result: the broadened-standpoint channels (especially female, country diversity) should be detectable in both strata but with different magnitudes—foreshadowing the interaction findings—while the core positive signs of the exposure and own-group channels hold across both, demonstrating the main effects are not artifacts of disciplinary composition.

column30: My rankings rest on a layered model in which opportunity, motivation, and temporal climate jointly determine whether a paper invokes racial-inequality language. The top tier reflects disciplinary jurisdiction: scholarly fields are institutionalized "ecologies" with their own legitimate objects of study, vocabularies, and reward structures, and racial inequality is a core, fundable, publishable object in the social sciences but largely outside the epistemic mandate of engineering and the natural sciences. This is why `social_science` (+) ranks first and `engineering_and_technology` (−) ranks third — they are essentially the positive and negative poles of the same structural sorting mechanism, with the negative pole slightly weaker because computer science's recent "algorithmic fairness/bias" turn smuggles some keyword hits back in. The second-ranked feature, `paper_inequality_mentions_3_years` (+), and the fifth, `news_inequality_mentions_3_years` (+), capture discursive opportunity structure over time: attention to inequality moves in waves driven by social movements and events (e.g., Black Lives Matter, 2020), and a rising ambient salience lowers the cost and raises the payoff of framing one's work in inequality terms, producing a bandwagon/agenda-setting dynamic. I rank the scholarly proxy above the news proxy because academic citation and topic cascades are the more proximate channel through which a given author decides what is "current" and citable, with media salience operating one step upstream. Underlying all of this are two assumptions: first, that the keyword-based label primarily captures explicit topical framing rather than latent substance, so features predicting the choice to name inequality (field norms, temporal fashion, authorial standpoint) matter more than features predicting underlying content; and second, that the strongest and most stable signals come from structural/contextual variables that are measured well (field, time-trend) rather than from demographic variables that are measured noisily.

Mixed, and genuinely informative. I'll separate what I got right from what surprised me.

What matched. My single strongest call held up: `social_science` (+) is #1, exactly as predicted, confirming that disciplinary jurisdiction is the dominant divider. The biggest surprise — my two temporal features vanished. I ranked `paper_inequality_mentions_3_years` at #2 and `news_inequality_mentions_3_years` at #5, and *neither* made the ML top five. In hindsight I think I made a classic error: I conflated *explaining the aggregate trend over time* with *discriminating among contemporaneous papers*. The ambient salience variables are essentially shared by every paper published in the same window, so even in a high-salience year like 2020 the overwhelming majority of papers still don't mention racial inequality — the temporal context tells you the base rate is rising but not *which* paper crosses the threshold. Random Forest's Gini importance rewards features that separate positives from negatives at the paper level, and a near-constant contextual variable simply can't do that. So my time-series intuition was substantively correct but predictively irrelevant for this cross-sectional task. That's the cleanest lesson here.

The second surprise — demographic/identity features dominate as a cluster, and I under-credited them. Three of the top five (`female_score` #2, `country_race_diversity_score` #3, `asian` #4) are author-composition variables I either omitted entirely or dismissed as too noisy. My reasoning about measurement error (the last-name→country→race pipeline) led me to *discount* these variables, but the model shows they carry strong signal despite the noise. More importantly, I applied the standpoint logic too narrowly — I attached it only to `black` and failed to generalize it.

- `female_score` (+) predicting *racial* inequality is the most theoretically interesting result. This is a cross-axis spillover I missed. It likely reflects an *intersectional / general social-justice orientation*: women in academia are overrepresented in inequality-attuned subfields and topics, so female authorship proxies "scholar working on social disadvantage broadly," not just gender. My model treated gender and racial standpoints as separate channels; the data suggest a shared latent "inequality orientation."

Authors from racially heterogeneous societies (the US above all, also Brazil, South Africa) are exposed to race as a salient social fact and are the dominant producers of racial-inequality scholarship. This is really an *exposure/context* mechanism operating at the level of the author's society rather than the team.

Net takeaway for my theory. The disciplinary-mandate layer was right and central. But I over-weighted *temporal climate* (which governs the trend, not paper-level discrimination) and under-weighted *author identity and societal exposure* (which do the cross-sectional work). This is the most instructive feedback yet, because it vindicates one half of my reasoning and cleanly overturns the other half — and the overturned half teaches a real lesson about *which kind* of interaction logic applies to *which kind* of variable.

What I got right, and why it's especially satisfying. My #1 prediction, `social_science × paper_inequality_mentions_3_years` (+), is confirmed exactly — same interaction, same sign, same rank. And `social_science × news_inequality_mentions_3_years` (+) is confirmed too, off by a single rank. What makes this gratifying is that it *resolves the apparent paradox from Race.11*: the temporal-salience variables dropped out of the main-effect top five, yet here they are at the very top of the interaction list. That is exactly the gating story I told — ambient salience can't discriminate among contemporaneous papers as a *main* effect (it's shared by everyone in the year), but its effect is concentrated where the field has a mandate to act on it, so it surfaces powerfully *in interaction with discipline*. So my "multiplicative gating" logic for **contextual/temporal** inputs was correct; it just lives at the interaction level rather than the main-effect level.

What surprised me — the sign flip on the demographic interaction. I predicted `social_science × black` (+) for my second slot, reasoning that disciplinary permission would *amplify* author standpoint. Instead the data show `female × social_science` with a **negative** sign. This contradicts my expectation in two ways: the standpoint variable that surfaces is `female` rather than `black`, and the interaction is sub-additive, not super-additive. I think my error was assuming a single universal interaction logic ("the field amplifies everything"). The negative sign points to a **substitution / saturation logic** instead, and on reflection it makes sense:

- Two partly redundant routes to the same outcome. Both being in social science and having female authors push a paper toward inequality framing. When one route is already "on," the other adds less. Inside social science the legitimacy to discuss race is already high (a near-ceiling), so additional female authorship has diminishing marginal returns; the response surface is concave, which mechanically produces a negative multiplicative term.
- Female authorship is more *diagnostic* outside social science. In medicine, education, or STEM-adjacent fields, a high female share specifically flags the subset of papers oriented toward diversity/equity/disparities work — so female authorship carries a large marginal effect *there*, where it is one of the few signals that a paper will invoke racial-diversity/bias language. Inside social science, plenty of papers discuss race regardless of author gender, so the female signal is less load-bearing. Hence the female effect is larger outside the field, i.e., a negative interaction with `social_science`.

Why `social_science × black` likely didn't appear. The `black` main effect was already weak and heavily attenuated by the race-imputation noise (#5), so its interaction is even noisier and gets crowded out — whereas the well-measured `female` variable is strong enough to surface, but it does so through substitution rather than amplification.

Net theoretical update. I need to abandon the assumption that disciplinary gating is uniformly *amplifying*. The correct, more differentiated picture is: **contextual/temporal inputs (the salience wave) interact super-additively with field** — they need the field to be activated, so the product term is positive — **whereas author-identity inputs interact sub-additively with field** — they are partial substitutes for the field's mandate and matter most where that mandate is absent, so the product term is negative. That distinction between complementary contextual inputs and substitutable identity inputs is the key thing I missed.
column54: My revised theory of interactions abandons the single, uniform logic I started with — "the discipline amplifies everything" — and replaces it with a two-logic framework distinguished by the nature of the interacting input, because the data show that disciplinary context combines with different variables in opposite ways. The organizing idea is that `social_science` functions as the master contextual moderator, but whether it amplifies or dampens another feature depends on whether that feature is a complement to the field's mandate or a substitute for it. The first logic is complementarity / super-additivity, which governs contextual-temporal inputs: the salience wave captured by `paper_inequality_mentions_3_years` and `news_inequality_mentions_3_years` cannot raise an individual paper's probability of discussing race on its own — ambient attention is shared by nearly all papers in a given window and is inert as a main effect — but it becomes potent precisely when it meets a field equipped to act on it. Social scientists are positioned to ride a rising tide of inequality attention (reframing projects, launching new ones, citing the moment), whereas technical fields are insulated, so the marginal effect of the wave is concentrated inside social science and the product terms `social_science × paper_inequality_mentions_3_years` and `social_science × news_inequality_mentions_3_years` are strongly positive. This vindicates and clarifies my original gating intuition: the temporal climate matters predictively only in interaction with field, which is why these terms top the interaction ranking even though the temporal main effects were weak. The second logic is substitution / saturation / sub-additivity, which governs author-identity inputs, and this is the part I had wrong. Both being in social science and having a high female author share are partially redundant routes to the same outcome — each independently pushes a paper toward inequality framing — so when one route is already active the other adds less. Inside social science the legitimacy to discuss race is already near a ceiling, making the response surface concave, so additional female authorship yields diminishing marginal returns; conversely, outside social science female authorship becomes highly diagnostic, flagging the specific subset of medical, educational, or STEM-adjacent papers oriented toward diversity and disparities, where it is one of the few signals that a paper will invoke racial-diversity or racial-bias language. The result is that the female effect is largest where the field's mandate is weakest, producing the empirically observed negative `female × social_science` interaction. Two further refinements follow. My revised theory makes four falsifiable claims about main effects: (1) disciplinary jurisdiction is the master sorter; (2) author identity is the primary paper-level engine, and the `female` effect reflects a *portable* inequality-orientation that operates across fields; (3) `country_race_diversity_score` captures a *societal-exposure* mechanism that should partly absorb the `asian` effect; and (4) temporal climate drives the aggregate rate but not paper-level discrimination. Each can be tested with the listed features plus `year_of_publication`.

Test 1 — Disciplinary dominance (regression). Fit a logit of the racial-inequality label on the three field dummies alone, then add all other features. Supporting result: `social_science` is strongly positive and `engineering_and_technology` strongly negative; the field block alone yields the largest single-block gain in pseudo-R²/AUC, and field coefficients remain large after adding demographics. This confirms field as the master sorter rather than a proxy for author composition.

Test 2 — Portability of the `female` / inequality-orientation effect (subgroup regression). Estimate the `female_score` coefficient *separately within each field* (social science, natural science, engineering). My theory says female authorship indexes a disposition that travels across fields and is most *diagnostic* where the field mandate is absent. Supporting result: the `female_score` coefficient is positive in all three subsamples and is *at least as large outside social science as inside it* (ideally larger in natural science/engineering). If instead the effect were positive only inside social science and ~zero elsewhere, my "portable orientation / substitution" claim would be falsified in favor of a pure within-field mechanism.

Test 3 — Societal exposure and the absorption of `asian` (nested regression). Run three models: (a) racial label on `asian` + field controls; (b) add `country_race_diversity_score`; (c) also add `authors_race_diversity_score`. Supporting result: `country_race_diversity_score` is positive and robust, and adding it in model (b) *substantially shrinks the `asian` coefficient* — demonstrating that `asian` was partly proxying authors-from-racially-diverse-societies. A further confirmation: `country_race_diversity_score` (per-author societal entropy) retains its effect even after controlling for `authors_race_diversity_score` (team entropy), showing exposure operates at the level of the author's society, not merely team composition.

Test 4 — Temporal climate: aggregate rate vs. cross-sectional inertness (two-level contrast). Part (i), aggregate: collapse to the year level and regress the yearly *share* of racial-inequality papers on `paper_inequality_mentions_3_years` / `news_inequality_mentions_3_years`; predict a strong positive longitudinal association. Part (ii), cross-sectional: in a paper-level logit *with year fixed effects*, the same two variables should add negligible AUC and carry near-zero coefficients, because they are nearly constant within a year. Supporting result: strong aggregate association but vanishing within-year discrimination — exactly the dissociation my theory predicts, explaining why these features lead the longitudinal trend yet drop out of the cross-sectional importance ranking.

Test 5 — Natural experiment: the Black Lives Matter salience shock (interrupted time series / pre–post). Use `year_of_publication` to define a post-shock indicator at the emergence of BLM (e.g., `post = 1` if year ≥ 2014, following Ferguson; 2013 as a robustness cut). Two predictions follow. First, an *interrupted-time-series* on the overall racial-inequality rate should show a discontinuous upward shift after 2014 — supporting Layer 3 (temporal climate moves the aggregate level). Second, and more important for the main-effects theory, re-estimate the author-identity coefficients (`female_score`, `black`, `country_race_diversity_score`) separately pre- and post-2014: if these are *structural dispositions*, their coefficients should be stable across the break while only the intercept/base rate jumps. Supporting result: a level shift in the base rate combined with stable identity slopes would confirm that the event shifts the climate while the author-identity engine is a constant structural force; a finding that the identity slopes themselves change substantially would instead suggest the shock reshaped *who* studies race, prompting a further revision.

Together, results in the predicted directions would corroborate the layered model — field as master sorter, portable author-identity as the paper-level engine, societal exposure underlying the racial-composition effects, and temporal climate as a level-shifting but non-discriminating force.

That cross-axis invariance is the headline, and it reframes how I should read my own performance.

On my prediction: my blind Q Gender.6 forecast repeated exactly the mistake I had not yet learned to avoid when I made it. I put `social_science × female` at #1 with a *positive* sign, reasoning that disciplinary permission would *amplify* the well-measured gender standpoint — and I was actually *more* confident about it for gender than for race. It came back at #3 with a *negative* sign. So as a blind prediction, this is a clear miss on both rank and sign.

But here is the important part: by the time I revised my racial interaction theory in Q Race.15, I had already replaced "the field amplifies everything" with a **two-logic framework** — contextual/temporal inputs *complement* the field (positive interaction, because they need the field to be activated), whereas author-identity inputs *substitute* for the field (negative interaction, because they supply inequality orientation where the field's mandate is weak). That revised theory, developed on the racial data, **predicts the gender results precisely.** So this is effectively an *out-of-sample confirmation*: the framework I built to explain one axis correctly forecasts the other. The gender data corroborate the revision even though they falsify my original blind guess.

Two things this teaches me beyond the racial case:

First, the substitution logic now holds for the **axis-matched, well-measured standpoint**. In the racial task I could partly hide behind measurement error — `black` was noisy, and the substituting variable was the cross-axis `female`. Here the substituting variable is `female` predicting *gender* inequality, the cleanest, most on-target, best-measured standpoint in the whole design — and it *still* interacts negatively with `social_science`. That rules out "measurement noise" as the explanation and confirms a genuine **structural saturation/substitution** mechanism: inside social science, gender gets discussed regardless of who writes the paper (a near-ceiling), so additional female authorship adds little; outside social science, a female-heavy author team is highly *diagnostic* of the specific papers that invoke gender-inequality language (e.g., women-in-STEM, female-authored medical or engineering work), so the female effect is largest exactly where the field mandate is absent.

Second, the **cross-axis invariance implies the interaction structure is a property of the science system itself, not of the topic.** The fact that race and gender produce identical interaction signatures suggests these patterns are generated by domain-general features — field as institutional permission, concave/ceiling response surfaces, and portable inequality-oriented dispositions that substitute for field — rather than by anything specific to racial versus gender discourse. That is a stronger and more general claim than I had been willing to make, and the data now support it.

Net: my blind gender forecast was wrong in the same way my blind racial forecast was, but my *revised* theory is now validated twice over. The update I carry forward is to treat the complement-versus-substitute distinction as a **general law of how disciplinary context combines with contextual versus identity inputs**, applicable across inequality axes, and to recognize that substitution applies even to the strongest, best-measured, on-axis standpoint variable.
column111: My updated theory of gender interactions is now the same two-logic framework I arrived at for race, and the gender evidence both confirms it and lets me state it more strongly as a domain-general principle. The organizing idea is that `social_science` acts as the master contextual moderator, but whether it amplifies or dampens another feature depends entirely on whether that feature is a complement to the field's mandate or a substitute for it. The first logic, complementarity / super-additivity, governs contextual–temporal inputs: the ambient salience captured by `paper_inequality_mentions_3_years` and `news_inequality_mentions_3_years` cannot lift an individual paper's probability of discussing gender on its own — it is shared by nearly all papers in a given window and is largely inert as a main effect — but it becomes potent precisely when it meets a field equipped to act on it. Social scientists are positioned to ride a rising tide of inequality attention (reframing projects, launching new ones, citing the moment, e.g., around #MeToo), whereas other fields are insulated, so the wave's marginal effect concentrates inside social science and the product terms `social_science × paper_inequality_mentions_3_years` (+) and `social_science × news_inequality_mentions_3_years` (+) are strongly positive and top the interaction ranking — exactly as observed, and exactly as in the racial model. This also resolves an apparent tension with the main-effects results: temporal climate is weak or borderline as a main effect yet leads the interaction ranking, because its predictive power is conditional on disciplinary activation rather than freestanding. The second logic, substitution / saturation / sub-additivity, governs author-identity inputs, and the gender evidence sharpens it decisively. Both being in social science and having a high female author share independently push a paper toward gender-inequality framing, so they are partially redundant routes to the same outcome; when one route is already active the other adds less. Inside social science, gender inequality is discussed near a ceiling regardless of author gender, making the response surface concave and giving additional female authorship diminishing returns; outside social science, a female-heavy team is highly diagnostic, flagging the specific subset of women-in-STEM, female-authored medical, or engineering-education papers that invoke gender-inequality language, so the female effect is largest exactly where the field mandate is weakest. The result is the empirically observed negative `female × social_science` interaction. The crucial refinement the gender data force is that this substitution logic is not an artifact of measurement error: in the racial model I could partly attribute the pattern to the noisy `black` variable and a cross-axis `female` substitute, but here the substituting variable is `female` predicting gender inequality — the cleanest, best-measured, perfectly on-axis standpoint in the design — and it still interacts negatively with field, proving the mechanism is genuine structural saturation rather than noise. Finally, the fact that race and gender produce identical interaction signatures (same three terms, same order, same signs) leads me to elevate the framework from an outcome-specific account to a general property of the science system: disciplinary context combines with contextual inputs as complements and with portable author-identity dispositions as substitutes, because field membership functions as institutional permission whose presence both enables the temporal wave and renders redundant the author's own orientation. The governing assumption of the updated theory is therefore that interaction sign is determined not by which inequality axis is at stake, nor by how well a feature is measured, but by the structural relationship between the feature and disciplinary legitimacy — complementary contextual forces yield positive interactions, substitutable identity dispositions yield negative ones — and that this holds invariantly across racial and gender discourse alike.

My revised gender theory makes four distinctive, falsifiable claims: (1) the negative disciplinary pole is *outcome-specific* — natural science, not engineering, because engineering has homegrown women-in-STEM discourse; (2) `female` is the strong, well-measured paper-level standpoint engine; (3) `asian` indexes a *portable, cross-axis* inequality-orientation rather than a gender-specific standpoint; and (4) temporal climate is a level-shifting force that edges into paper-level relevance only because the #MeToo shock is sharp. Each is testable with the listed features plus `year_of_publication`, and several gain power because we have *both* outcome labels.

Test 1 — The engineering-rehabilitation claim (cross-outcome field contrast). This is the flagship gender-specific test. Estimate the field coefficients in the gender model and the racial model and compare them directly (pool both outcomes and test a field × outcome interaction). Supporting result: `natural_science` is significantly negative for gender, while `engineering_and_technology` is *not* the negative pole for gender (near zero or positive) — and crucially, the engineering coefficient is significantly *more favorable for gender than for race*. That cross-outcome gap is the signature of a topic-specific internal discourse (women-in-STEM) rehabilitating engineering for the gender axis only. If engineering were equally negative for both axes, the "outcome-specific negative pole" claim is falsified.

Test 2 — Female as a robust, portable standpoint engine (subgroup regression). Estimate the `female_score` coefficient overall with field controls, then *separately within each field*. Supporting result: `female_score` is large and positive overall, survives field controls (so it is not merely a proxy for being in social science), and remains positive *within natural science and engineering*, not only within social science. A positive female effect inside engineering specifically would corroborate the women-in-STEM channel; a female effect confined to social science would suggest a narrower, field-bound mechanism.

Test 3 — `asian` as a portable cross-axis orientation, partly absorbed by societal exposure (nested + cross-outcome). First, confirm `asian` is positive in *both* the gender and racial models (cross-axis consistency). Then run nested gender models: (a) gender label on `asian` + field; (b) add `country_race_diversity_score`; (c) add `authors_race_diversity_score`. Supporting result: `asian` is positive for both outcomes, and in the gender model its coefficient *shrinks substantially once `country_race_diversity_score` is added* — indicating it proxies authors situated in racially diverse, inequality-salient societies rather than a gender-specific standpoint. This mirrors the racial absorption test and unifies the interpretation across axes.

Test 4 — Shared latent inequality-orientation (cross-prediction correlation). Build two paper-level predicted probabilities using *only the author-identity features* (`female_score`, `asian`, `country_race_diversity_score`, `authors_race_diversity_score`): one trained to predict the gender label, one the racial label. Compute the correlation of these two predicted scores across papers. Supporting result: a strong positive correlation — i.e., the author profiles that predict gender-inequality framing are largely the same profiles that predict racial-inequality framing — which is exactly what a single portable "inequality-oriented author" construct implies, as opposed to two independent axis-matched standpoints.

Test 5 — Temporal climate: aggregate vs. paper level, and the #MeToo sharpness (two-level + natural experiment). Part (i), aggregate: regress the yearly gender-inequality *share* on `paper_inequality_mentions_3_years`; predict a strong positive trend. Part (ii), cross-sectional with year fixed effects: predict the same variable adds little within-year discrimination. Part (iii), the gender-specific prediction: compare the *within-year incremental contribution* of `paper_inequality_mentions_3_years` across the gender and racial models; predict it is *larger for gender*, explaining why this feature surfaced in the gender main-effect top five but not the racial one. Part (iv), natural experiment: define `post = 1` if `year ≥ 2017` (#MeToo) and run an interrupted-time-series on the overall gender-inequality rate. Supporting result: a sharp, discontinuous upward break at 2017 — sharper than the more gradual post-2014 rise in the racial series — combined with *stable* `female_score` and `asian` slopes estimated pre- and post-2017 (only the intercept jumps). That pattern would confirm the dual claim that temporal climate shifts the *level* while the author-identity engine is a structurally stable force, and that the sharpness of the gender shock is what gives the temporal feature its modest paper-level traction.

Across all five, the corroborating pattern is the same one I expect for race — **mediation, absorption, and cross-axis convergence rather than reversal**: field as outcome-specific institutional permission, a portable author-identity disposition shared across inequality axes as the paper-level engine, societal exposure underlying the racial-composition effects, and temporal climate as a sharp-shock-dependent level shifter rather than a paper-level discriminator.

Q Gender.17 — Testing the gender theory with additional (currently unavailable) variables

The gender theory has four distinctive claims that the current features can only proxy crudely: the engineering-rehabilitation (women-in-STEM) mechanism, the portable cross-axis author disposition, the societal-exposure logic, and a temporal channel that is currently pooled across all inequality forms rather than gender-specific. The new variables I'd most want are the ones that let me test these directly rather than by inference.

1. Axis-matched (gender-specific) salience series. This is the most valuable addition and is unique to making the temporal claim rigorous. The existing `news_inequality_mentions` and `paper_inequality_mentions` pool gender, racial, and economic inequality together. Use: substitute a gender-specific media/scholarly salience series (e.g., volume of #MeToo-era gender-equity coverage) for the pooled measure and horse-race them. Supporting result: gender-inequality framing tracks the gender-specific series far more tightly than the pooled one, and the gender-specific series produces the sharp 2017 break — confirming that the temporal mechanism is topic-matched and that the modest paper-level traction I observed comes from a sharp, axis-specific shock rather than generic inequality attention.

2. Author prior cross-axis publication history. This is the direct, decisive test of my "portable inequality-oriented author" construct. Use: for each author, compute the share of their prior papers on gender topics and, separately, on racial topics; enter both into the gender model. Supporting result: prior gender history strongly predicts current gender framing (a disposition) and substantially mediates the `female` and `asian` effects; crucially, prior racial-topic history also positively predicts current gender framing. That cross-axis carryover — authors who studied race becoming more likely to frame work in gender terms — is exactly what a single shared disposition implies and what two independent axis-matched standpoints would not.

3. Fine-grained subfield within engineering and STEM. My engineering-rehabilitation claim attributes the field's non-negativity to a specific internal discourse, which coarse buckets can't isolate. Use: split engineering/CS into subfields (engineering education, human–computer interaction, "women in computing"/diversity venues, versus mechanical, civil, electrical). Supporting result: the positive gender signal inside engineering concentrates in the education/HCI/diversity subfields, while core technical subfields remain near-zero — demonstrating that rehabilitation is driven by pockets of women-in-STEM discourse rather than engineering writ large, and pinpointing the mechanism behind Test 1 in Q Gender.16.

4. Societal gender-equality context of the author's actual affiliation country. The genuine gender analog of `country_race_diversity_score` (which is race-only). Use: attach a national gender-context index (e.g., a gender-gap/gender-inequality measure) for each author's country of residence/affiliation, and test it controlling for resources/field. Supporting result: a positive effect of working in a society where gender inequality is a salient public issue — paralleling the racial societal-exposure finding — would show the exposure mechanism generalizes across axes. (I'd also test the competing "academic-capacity" account, in which wealthy egalitarian countries publish more such work; distinguishing salience-exposure from capacity is itself a valuable contrast.)

5. Verified author gender and career stage. `female` is well-measured but still probabilistic, and main-effect strength may vary by seniority. Use: replace imputed gender with self-identified gender, and add academic age/seniority. Supporting result: the female effect is robust or strengthens with verified gender (ruling out residual measurement attenuation), and is moderated by career stage in a theoretically interpretable way (e.g., stronger among established women with latitude to choose topics, or among junior cohorts reflecting pipeline change) — refining the standpoint mechanism beyond a single static slope.

6. Venue mission and gender-relevant funding. The disciplinary main effect is theorized as concrete institutional permission. Use: add journal mission/special-issue indicators and gender-relevant funding availability by year, and test whether the `social_science` main effect attenuates once these are controlled and whether funding shocks lift gender framing most where the mandate already exists. Supporting result: the raw field effect shrinks once venue and funding enter — showing "discipline" is shorthand for legitimacy and incentive structures — corroborating the same complementarity logic across the gender axis.

Across all six, the corroborating signature mirrors the racial case and unifies the two: the more proximate, better-measured variables (axis-matched salience, prior cross-axis history, fine subfield, verified gender, venue/funding) should absorb and explain the crude proxies I now rely on, while preserving the layered structure — field as outcome-specific institutional permission, a portable author disposition shared across inequality axes as the paper-level engine, societal context underlying the demographic effects, and a topic-matched, shock-driven temporal climate that shifts the level rather than discriminating among contemporaneous papers. The single strongest confirmation would be Test 2's cross-axis carryover, since a portable disposition is the keystone claim that ties my racial and gender theories into one account.

column30: My ranking reflects a hierarchy of structural, epistemic, and contextual drivers shaping the likelihood that a paper discusses racial inequality. At the top, `social_science` is paramount because disciplinary paradigms fundamentally structure research agendas: social science fields possess the theoretical frameworks (e.g., critical race theory, stratification research), methodological training, and journal ecosystems that normalize racial inequality as a legitimate object of inquiry, whereas STEM fields typically foreground technical or natural phenomena. Second, `black` captures standpoint epistemology and lived experience: scholars estimated to be Black may be more likely to center racial inequality due to community-engaged scholarship, epistemic traditions in Black sociology, or personal motivation to address systemic injustice—even after accounting for discipline. Third, `paper_inequality_mentions_3_years` reflects path dependence in academic discourse: fields, networks, or journals with recent inequality scholarship generate citation momentum, special issues, and shared vocabularies that lower entry barriers for new work on racial inequality. Fourth, `authors_race_diversity_score` signals that racially heterogeneous teams may bring intersectional perspectives, cross-disciplinary collaborations (e.g., social science + CS on algorithmic bias), or explicit equity commitments that increase the salience of racial inequality keywords. Fifth, `hispanic_and_other` extends the standpoint logic to other marginalized racial/ethnic groups whose research may engage immigration, colonization, or multi-ethnic stratification. I assign positive signs to all five based on the assumption that structural positionality (discipline, author race), discursive momentum, and team composition collectively increase the probability that racial inequality appears in titles or abstracts. Key caveats include measurement error in race estimation, potential confounding between race and discipline, and the possibility that effects strengthen in later time periods as racial justice discourse became more institutionalized post-2010s.

Viewing the ML results prompts both validation and theoretical refinement. On one hand, my top prediction—`social_science` (+) as the strongest predictor—is confirmed, reinforcing the centrality of disciplinary infrastructure in shaping racial inequality discourse. Similarly, `black` (+) appearing in the top 5 aligns with standpoint epistemology expectations. However, three notable divergences invite reflection:

First, `female_score` ranking #2 (+) for *racial* inequality prediction was unexpected; I had prioritized it for gender inequality but underestimated cross-topic spillover. This suggests women scholars may engage with multiple axes of inequality simultaneously—perhaps due to intersectional research agendas, broader commitments to social justice, or greater likelihood of working in interdisciplinary teams where racial inequality is salient. Second, `country_race_diversity_score` (+) outranking `authors_race_diversity_score` implies that macro-level contextual exposure (e.g., scholars trained in or migrating from racially heterogeneous societies) may shape research agendas more powerfully than team composition alone—a nuance my theory underemphasized. Third, `asian` (+) appearing in the top 5 challenges my assumption that racial inequality scholarship is primarily driven by Black or Hispanic scholars; this may reflect Asian scholars' engagement with racialization, immigration, model minority discourse, or comparative race frameworks, particularly in post-2010s contexts of rising anti-Asian violence.

Conversely, `paper_inequality_mentions_3_years` not appearing in the ML top 5 suggests I may have overestimated path dependence relative to author-level and contextual factors. These divergences likely stem from (a) my theoretical focus on U.S.-centric disciplinary norms, whereas the Semantic Scholar corpus is global; (b) measurement differences (e.g., country-level vs. team-level diversity); and (c) the ML model capturing non-linear or interactive effects that my linear theoretical reasoning did not fully anticipate. Overall, these results encourage a more nuanced theory that integrates author standpoint, national context, and cross-inequality scholarly engagement.

The gender interaction results are striking in that they are identical in structure to the racial interaction results: the same three interactions, the same ranks, and the same signs. My top two predictions are confirmed—social_science × paper_inequality_mentions_3_years (+) at rank 1 and the closely related social_science × news_inequality_mentions_3_years (+) at rank 2—both vindicating the amplification logic I proposed: discursive opportunity, whether academic or in the news, converts into gender-inequality scholarship most readily where the disciplinary environment makes the topic actionable. I had ranked female × paper_inequality_mentions third; instead news attention took that slot, but the substitution is theoretically minor since both express the same context-gates-opportunity mechanism.

The genuine surprise—again mirroring race—is female × social_science (–), which contradicts my predicted positive complementarity. I had assumed standpoint motivation and disciplinary legitimacy reinforce each other; the negative sign instead points to substitution. Outside social science (engineering, computing, medicine), a high female share is a rare and strongly distinguishing signal that a paper engages gender inequality, because such work is unusual and selected there. Inside social science, gender inequality is already broadly accessible regardless of author gender, so the marginal lift from female authorship shrinks. Each factor matters most where the other is absent.

What I find most theoretically significant is the cross-outcome consistency: the very same amplification-plus-substitution interaction architecture governs both racial- and gender-inequality discussion. This suggests the interaction structure is not topic-specific but reflects a general logic of how academic inequality discourse is produced—disciplinary context amplifies external discursive opportunity but substitutes for internal author-composition signals—strengthening my confidence that this is a robust structural feature rather than an artifact of either outcome.
column111: The second-order interaction structure governing gender-inequality discussion is best understood through two distinct logics—amplification and substitution—that apply to different pairs of features, and notably the same architecture governs racial-inequality discussion, suggesting a general rather than topic-specific logic of how academic inequality discourse is produced. The dominant logic is amplification between disciplinary context and discursive opportunity: the marginal effect of recent attention to inequality, whether academic (paper_inequality_mentions_3_years) or in the broader public sphere (news_inequality_mentions_3_years), is realized most strongly within social science, because only there is the topic conceptually actionable and legitimate. Social science fields function as the conversion mechanism that translates a favorable intellectual and media climate into actual gender-inequality scholarship, so both social_science × paper_inequality_mentions and social_science × news_inequality_mentions are positive. This also explains why paper_inequality_mentions, though it did surface as a main effect for gender, exerts much of its influence conditionally—its predictive power is concentrated where disciplinary receptivity exists rather than operating uniformly across the corpus. The second logic, which I underestimated, is substitution between disciplinary context and author standpoint: female × social_science is negative because field-level legitimation and individual-author disposition are partially redundant routes to the same outcome. Where the field already makes gender inequality broadly accessible, the additional predictive lift from female authorship diminishes; conversely, outside social science—in engineering, computing, or medicine—a high female share becomes a rare and strongly distinguishing signal that a paper engages gender inequality. My original complementarity assumption (that standpoint motivation needs disciplinary legitimacy to be expressed) was therefore only half right: complementarity holds between disciplinary context and external discursive opportunity, but substitution holds between context and internal author-composition signals, because once a topic is broadly legitimated by the field, individual-author markers become less marginally necessary and thus less predictive. The cross-outcome identity of this interaction structure strengthens my confidence that it reflects a robust, general feature of academic knowledge production rather than an artifact specific to either gender or race.

If asian's effect attenuates sharply once country diversity is controlled, and/or is not concentrated in any gender-relevant field but spread structurally, this favors the exposure interpretation. Supporting result: partial attenuation of asian under diversity controls, with no gender-specific field concentration—consistent with a structural rather than standpoint mechanism.

**Test 3 — Natural-experiment / temporal interaction using a societal shock.** Code post = 1 for year_of_publication ≥ 2017 (capturing the post-#MeToo surge in gender-inequality salience) and 0 otherwise. The discursive-opportunity logic predicts the post-shock rise in gender-inequality discussion is concentrated where the topic is legitimate. column30: My ranking reflects a simple causal hierarchy in which disciplinary context dominates, discourse environment amplifies, and author standpoint selects. Discipline comes first because the corpus spans fields with radically different objects of study, and racial inequality is constitutively a social-science problem—the concepts, methods, and journals that even permit such keywords are concentrated in sociology, political science, and psychology—so social_science is the strongest positive signal and engineering_and_technology its mirror image: these fields' epistemic agenda (systems, formalisms, devices) almost never engages racialized social relations, making it a powerful negative predictor. (I rank engineering above natural_science as the negative because it is the largest "never-discusses-race" bloc in a corpus heavy with CS, math, and engineering.) Next I place the two lagged discourse measures, invoking an agenda-setting / issue-attention logic: scholarship is responsive to the salience of inequality in the surrounding intellectual and public sphere, so when academic and news attention to inequality has been high in the prior three years (e.g., the post-Ferguson/BLM period), the supply of and receptivity to racial-inequality papers rises—both positive. I rank paper_inequality_mentions above news because academic publishing responds more directly and with shorter lag to its own field's attention cycles than to general news, though the two are correlated. Finally, black author share enters as a positive but lower-ranked predictor via a standpoint and topic-selection mechanism: scholars who have lived experience of, or community proximity to, racial disadvantage are disproportionately likely to choose it as an object of study. I rank it last and modest in magnitude for two reasons—the name-and-country-based inference is noisy and the base rate of Black authors in the corpus is low, both of which attenuate the observable association—so while theoretically central, its predictive contribution should be smaller than the structural discipline and discourse signals above it.
